turns.prompt_text: What is a Nas like a hard drive storage system or SSD system?
turns.response_html:
A NAS (Network Attached Storage) isn't actually a specific type of storage media like an HDD or an SSD. Instead, it is an independent, dedicated storage appliance that connects directly to a local network (usually via Ethernet to a router or switch) rather than plugging into a single computer via USB.

Think of a NAS as a secure, private mini-server whose sole job is to store files and serve them to every authorized device on the network simultaneously.

As seen in the diagram above, instead of locking data down to one specific computer, the NAS acts as a centralized node that all local machines can access over the network.

The Storage Media: HDD vs. SSD

Inside a NAS enclosure, there are drive bays where actual storage drives are inserted. A NAS can run on either mechanical hard drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), or a combination of both.

The choice between them depends entirely on the workload needs:

FeatureHDDs in a NASSSDs in a NAS
Best ForMassive data archives, cold storage, media libraries, and system backups.High-IOPS workflows, virtual machines, running local containers/databases, and silent environments.
Cost EfficiencyLow cost per gigabyte; ideal for high-capacity multi-terabyte setups.Higher cost per gigabyte, but prices continue to narrow for lower capacities.
Performance LimitLimited by physical platter read/write speeds.Typically limited by network bandwidth (e.g., standard 1GbE network caps transfers at roughly 115 MB/s, bottlenecks an SSD).

Hybrid Setups: Many modern NAS devices utilize large HDDs for bulk storage capacity alongside a pair of fast M.2 NVMe SSDs configured strictly as a read/write cache to speed up random access performance.

How it Differs from Other Storage

  • DAS (Direct Attached Storage): A standard external hard drive or SSD. It plugs directly into a machine via USB/Thunderbolt. Only that machine can access it natively.
  • NAS (Network Attached Storage): Operates over the local network protocol (SMB, NFS, or AFP). It runs its own lightweight operating system, handles logical data management (like RAID arrays), and remains accessible even if every other computer in the house is turned off.
  • Cloud Storage: Off-site storage managed by a third party. A NAS provides a similar "access anywhere" capability if configured for remote access, but the user retains absolute ownership, data privacy, and zero monthly subscription fees.

turns.prompt_text: I have a bunch of hard drives and SSDI sitting in my apartment at Ames. How would I make an Nas out of that? But I have to connect it to another some kind of smaller computer like a pie or water pipito with
turns.response_html:
Building a custom NAS out of a mismatched collection of spare hard drives and SSDs using a single-board computer (SBC) like a Raspberry Pi or a similar clone is a fantastic weekend project. It gives you complete data ownership and breathes new life into old hardware.

However, a scrap-drive build using an SBC has two major pitfalls that trip up almost everyone: power limitations and mismatched capacities.

The Two Golden Rules for SBC NAS Builds

Rule 1: Never power multiple drives directly from the Pi. A Raspberry Pi's USB ports cannot output enough amperage to spin up mechanical hard drives or sustain multiple SSD read/write peaks. Trying to do so will cause low-voltage warnings, drive dropouts, and filesystem corruption. You must use an externally powered USB 3.0 hub or an external multi-bay USB enclosure.

Rule 2: Forget traditional RAID. Traditional hardware or software RAID (like RAID 5) requires drives to be identical in size and speed. Mixing HDDs and SSDs of varying sizes breaks standard arrays. Instead, you will use storage pooling software to virtually stitch the drives together.

The Architecture: mergerfs + SnapRAID

The ideal software stack for a pile of random drives on Linux is combining mergerfs with SnapRAID:

  • mergerfs: Pools drives of any size or type into a single, unified mount point (e.g., three random drives appear to your network as one massive folder). It doesn't strip data across drives, meaning if one drive dies, the data on the other drives remains completely intact.
  • SnapRAID: A backup/parity tool for home servers. You dedicate your single largest drive as a "parity drive," and it calculates recovery data to protect you if any other single drive fails.

A Quick Word on SSD Optimization

Because standard SBC networks usually max out at Gigabit speeds (~115 MB/s), a fast SSD will be bottlenecked by the network cable if used for sequential file transfers. To extract the best value from your SSDs in this setup, use them to run Docker containers, local databases, or media server configurations (like Plex/Jellyfin), where random read/write speeds and low latency matter far more than raw network throughput.
